special_requirements: ELIGIBILITY (favorable for foreign applicants): 'All responsible sources from academia, industry and the research community worldwide may submit proposals under this BAA.' This is the ONR Long Range BAA and it explicitly covers ONR Global (ONRG) - 'Unless indicated otherwise, any references to ONR within the BAA refers to ONR, ONRG and MCWL.' INELIGIBLE: Federally Funded Research & Development Centers (FFRDCs) including DOE National Laboratories are NOT eligible to receive awards (teaming with eligible prime Offerors is allowed if permitted by the sponsoring agreement). Navy laboratories, military universities and warfare centers, and other DoD and civilian agency laboratories are NOT eligible and should not directly submit white papers or full proposals. University Affiliated Research Centers (UARCs) ARE eligible unless precluded by their DoD UARC contract. HARD STATUTORY BAR: per NDAA 2021 Section 1062, beginning October 1, 2023, DoD may not fund institutions of higher education that host a Confucius Institute (a cultural institute directly or indirectly funded by the Government of the People's Republic of China), other than amounts provided directly to students as education assistance, unless a waiver is provided. FOREIGN INFLUENCE SCREEN: as part of the Naval relevance criterion, per NDAA FY2019 Sec 1286 as amended by NDAA 2021 Sec 1299C, ONR assesses risk from Foreign Talent Recruitment Programs, Funding Sources, Patent Filings, and Associations/Affiliations with persons or entities on the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security Denied Entity Lists. Disclosures of current and pending support may render an applicant ineligible. REGISTRATION: must be registered in SAM prior to submission, provide a valid UEI, and obtain a CAGE Code (foreign entities obtain an NCAGE code); maintain active SAM registration throughout. Cover Page is MANDATORY for ONR and ONRG - FedConnect will not accept a white paper without it, and ONRG requires the Science Director / Program Officer information as a required field. Use Agency Routing Number Code 600 for ONRG on the SF-424; applicants who fail to provide a Program Officer Code identifier may have their proposal rejected. Grants are single-PI awards. Grants do not include delivery of software, prototypes, or other hardware deliverables. A non-proprietary version of the Statement of Work must be submitted for all proposals. Attachments must be PDF, no macros, not password protected, or they fail ONR's automated acceptance check and are rejected. EVALUATION CRITERIA (equally weighted, no point scores published): (1) Overall scientific and technical merits of the proposal and responsiveness to the topic; (2) Potential Naval relevance and contribution to the ONR and Department of Navy mission; (3) The availability of funds (not applicable to white papers). COST SHARE: not required for grants; note an OTA for research shall provide for a 50/50 cost share to the maximum extent practicable (OTAs are covered by Appendix 2, not the grants appendix).

special_requirements: ELIGIBILITY: For IDA resources the applicant must be a U.S. or non-U.S. NGO including private voluntary organizations (PVOs). For Title II emergency resources the applicant must be a PVO or a cooperative. INELIGIBLE APPLICANTS: USAID will not accept applications from or provide resources to individuals, parastatal organizations, or U.S. Government departments and agencies under these Guidelines for IDA or Title II resources. NON-COMPETITIVE: these Guidelines apply only to applications for non-competitive awards; competitive emergency awards are issued under a separate Annual Program Statement. Submission is via the BHA Application and Award Management Portal (AAMP), not Grants.gov - AAMP credentials must be requested in advance from BHA.AAMP@usaid.gov, and first-time applicants must also request creation of an awardee organizational profile. Emailed, hard-copy, or faxed applications are not accepted except in extenuating circumstances. UEI required (replaced DUNS). Activities longer than 18 months require prior consultation with BHA staff and strong justification. Section 9 imposes ineligible goods and services, ineligible suppliers, restricted goods (agricultural commodities, livestock, seeds, fertilizers, pesticides, pharmaceuticals, motor vehicles, covered technologies, used equipment), and prohibited source countries / U.S. economic sanctions / export restrictions that can make a proposed activity or procurement ineligible. Annex D lists high-risk environments requiring additional requirements; the entire country of Ukraine was added 3/4/2022. Sphere standards should be applied and non-adherence must be strongly justified. Sectors are restricted to a fixed BHA list (Agriculture; Economic Recovery and Market Systems; Food Assistance; Health; Humanitarian Coordination, Information Management, and Assessments; Humanitarian Policy, Studies, Analysis, or Applications; Logistics Support; Monitoring and Evaluation; Multipurpose Cash Assistance; Natural Hazards and Technological Risks; Nutrition; Protection; Disaster Risk Reduction Policy and Practice; Shelter and Settlements; Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene). Mandatory cross-cutting elements: Age and Disability; Disaster Risk Reduction Mainstreaming; Gender Analysis and Integration; Gender-Based Violence Risk Mitigation; Local Capacity Building; Natural Resource Management; Protection Mainstreaming; Response Analysis; Structure/Infrastructure Construction and Analysis. NOTE: USAID was dissolved as an independent agency in 2025 and its programs were absorbed into the Department of State; this guidance document is the last agency-published version and its operative status should be confirmed before use.

special_requirements: ADMINISTERED BY DOL/ETA, NOT BY ARC. Despite the ARC branding, WORC is a Department of Labor Employment and Training Administration competition under Assistance Listing 17.280, WIOA Dislocated Worker National Reserve Demonstration Grants, authorized by WIOA Section 169(c). Applications go to grants.gov against the DOL FOA, NOT to ARC Pathways and NOT through an ARC state program manager. ARC, the Delta Regional Authority, and the Northern Border Regional Commission are partner regional commissions, not the awarding agency. CURRENT ROUND: WORC Round 7, FOA-ETA-26-23, closing July 23, 2026 at 11:59 PM Eastern. Approximately $49,200,000 for approximately 6-24 grants; awards range $2,000,000 to $8,000,000. REQUIRED PARTNERSHIPS ARE AN EFFECTIVE ELIGIBILITY GATE: applicants must identify, at a minimum, (1) at least three employers or industry/trade associations for EACH proposed industry sector, (2) at least one Workforce Development Entity administering the public workforce system under WIOA, (3) at least one public or private Education/Training Provider, and (4) the State Apprenticeship Agency if Registered Apprenticeships are proposed in a state with a federally recognized SAA. An applicant may only represent ONE required partnership role. Applicants that fail to provide signed documentation of commitment from ALL required employer partners will receive ZERO POINTS on the 20-point Sector Partnership and Industry Engagement rating factor - and LETTERS OF SUPPORT ARE EXPLICITLY NOT SUFFICIENT to satisfy this factor; signed letters of commitment, MOUs, or partnership agreements are needed. Documentation must state the partner's roles, responsibilities, and contributions. Projects must focus on at least one of these sectors: skilled trades/construction, health care, information technology, manufacturing, domestic energy production, or business/professional services occupations. All participants must live or work within a community in the WORC regions; eligible participant categories are new entrants to the workforce, dislocated workers, and incumbent workers. FOR-PROFIT ENTITIES ARE NOT ELIGIBLE APPLICANTS, though for-profit education/training providers may be partner organizations, and earning of profit is not an allowable cost for recipients or sub-recipients. Veterans' priority of service under 38 U.S.C. 4215 applies. Cost caps: supportive services capped at 10 percent of grant funds; incentive payments capped at 1.5 percent; equipment and minor alterations capped at 15 percent or $100,000, whichever is less, and require prior Grant Officer approval; salary and bonus rates may not exceed Executive Level II. All work-based learning participants must be PAID. special_requirements: NOT A COMPETITIVE GRANT AND NOT OPEN TO MOST ORGANIZATIONS. National Dislocated Worker Grants (Assistance Listing 17.277, WIOA Section 170) are non-competitive, event-triggered discretionary awards. There is no scored review, no rating factors, and no annual competition. ELIGIBLE APPLICANTS ARE NARROW: states, outlying areas, Indian tribal governments as defined by the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act, and WIOA Section 166-eligible entities. A local nonprofit or a local government generally CANNOT apply directly - it participates as a subrecipient or project operator under the state's grant, so the practical first step is contacting the state workforce agency, not grants.gov. TWO-STAGE TIMING GATE FOR DISASTER RECOVERY: an emergency application may only be submitted when BOTH (1) a qualifying disaster declaration by FEMA or another federal agency with jurisdiction is made within 45 business days of the date of the emergency or disaster event, AND (2) the emergency application is submitted not more than 15 business days after the qualifying declaration. ETA will award no more than $1 million following approval of an emergency application, so the SF-424 must indicate no more than a $1 million federal funding request at that stage. If an emergency application is submitted, the FULL application is due within 60 business days of receipt of the initial award. Period of performance is up to 36 months; a shorter period must be stated. Disaster Recovery applicants must name the state emergency management agency or FEMA contact with whom they have or will coordinate to avoid duplication of effort. For emergencies or disasters of national significance declared by a federal agency OTHER than FEMA, the application must include information demonstrating the projected level of job loss (at least 50 jobs) in the disaster area. EMPLOYMENT RECOVERY PREREQUISITE: WIOA requires that Rapid Response or other early intervention activities occur BEFORE an Employment Recovery DWG application is submitted, and the application must describe those efforts and their results - an applicant that has not run Rapid Response first is not ready to apply. Qualifying-event documentation such as a WARN notice or other layoff documentation is required. If a funding request exceeds ETA's published funding limitations, additional justification MUST be submitted. Awards must comply with WIOA statute and regulations including DWG regulations at 20 CFR part 687, TEGL 09-24, grant award terms and conditions, and Uniform Guidance at 2 CFR parts 200 and 2900. The grants.gov listing for the current guidance posting (ETA-TEGL-09-24) showed a close date of May 8, 2026, but this is a rolling programmatic posting rather than a competition deadline - applications are driven by qualifying events, so verify the currently posted DWG guidance on grants.gov before relying on that date. Overall program scale in the listing: $300,000,000 across roughly 150 awards, $150,000 minimum to $10,000,000 maximum. Program contact: DOL-ETA-DWG@dol.gov.

special_requirements: CURRENT ROUND: TBCP Round 3, Funding Opportunity Number 2026-NTIA-TBCP, Assistance Listing 11.029. Complete applications must be received no later than 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on September 17, 2026. Up to $540,000,000 available. Submit via grants.gov (strongly encouraged), email to TBCP3@ntia.gov, or postal mail/courier; facsimile is not accepted; partial or duplicate applications using multiple transmission methods will not be accepted. HARD ELIGIBILITY: only a Tribal Government, a Tribal College or University, the Department of Hawaiian Home Lands on behalf of the Native Hawaiian Community, a Tribal organization, or an Alaska Native Corporation may receive a grant. A non-Tribal nonprofit, city, county, or ISP cannot be the applicant. SINGLE APPLICATION RULE: an Eligible Entity may submit ONLY ONE application, which must include the total amount of funding requested and account for ALL projects that will use that funding - a second application is not an option, so the entity must consolidate everything into one submission. EITHER/OR RULE: an Eligible Entity may apply for Broadband Use and Adoption funding OR Broadband Infrastructure Deployment funding, BUT NOT BOTH - this choice determines which of the two entirely different narrative structures and which assurance form (SF-424B vs SF-424D) applies. All proposed projects should be comprehensive and NOT reliant on future funding or a future adjacent project. EQUITABLE DISTRIBUTION: NTIA will allocate up to $500,000 to each Federally Recognized Tribe delineated by the Bureau of Indian Affairs, awarded only to Tribal Governments that have NOT previously received a TBCP award in prior rounds; for consortium or regional applications, the per-Tribe equitable distribution flows to the consortium lead applicant. Applicants that did not receive a round 1 or round 2 award MUST also describe what they would do if they received only the $500,000 equitable distribution - a fallback scope is effectively mandatory. Target award ranges: $500,000 to $2,500,000 for Use and Adoption; $1,000,000 to $25,000,000 for Infrastructure Deployment; requests outside the range require a compelling written justification. ADMINISTRATIVE COST CAP: administrative costs are capped BY STATUTE at 2 percent of the grant amount, counting direct AND indirect administrative costs combined, and the budget narrative must show the calculation. Applicants without an existing NICRA may charge the 15 percent de minimis rate under 2 C.F.R. 200.414; a NICRA MUST be used if the applicant receives more than $35,000,000 in federal funding in its fiscal year or already has one. Infrastructure deployment must prioritize unserved Native American/Alaska Native/Native Hawaiian households (not currently receiving 25/3 Mbps or greater with latency considerations) that are not subject to an enforceable buildout commitment. Applicants must disclose all other federal/state/outside funding applied for or received (BEAD, Capital Projects Fund, prior TBCP, any other federal broadband grant) and certify there will be no duplicative funding. Applications must be complete, in English, and in the required format - NTIA WILL NOT CONSIDER applications that fail to comply or are untimely.

Eligible applicants are limited to state or territorial governments - specifically the State Administrative Agency (SAA) or the state's Emergency Management Agency (EMA). Subapplicants and subawards ARE allowed, so a nonprofit could in principle be a subrecipient through the state EMA/SAA, but the state is the applicant of record and there is no direct federal application path. Before submitting the Work Plan, the applicant MUST work with the FEMA Regional Administrator (RA) or designated Regional EMPG Program Manager to identify three-to-five priority areas that serve as the focus for EMPG-funded investments; the priorities must be mutually agreed to by the applicant and the RA and should be driven by the THIRA/SPR process outputs and other sources (AARs, audit and monitoring findings, Hazard Mitigation Plans, other deliberate planning products) and reflect the recipient's IPP. Applicants must set at least one performance goal for each RA agreed-upon priority area; each goal must be specific, measurable, achievable within the period of performance, relevant to the priority area, and have a target date for completion (SMART), must describe how achieving it will impact the priority area, and must include an estimate quantifying the extent to which the supporting investments will close capability gaps (NOFO example: 'Increase the percentage of people who can find and secure long-term housing by 10% within 1 year of an incident'). The Regional Administrator must APPROVE the final Work Plan before states may draw down EMPG funds - grant funds are released only upon approval. After approval, any changes to the approved Work Plan, including changes in project scope and budget changes within any direct cost category exceeding 10% of the total award amount, require advance approval from the RA or designated Regional EMPG Program Manager (2 C.F.R. 200.308). Narrative content in the Work Plan template is deliberately minimized - many cells use dropdowns for selecting applicable data. special_requirements: NONPROFITS CAN APPLY, but only a specific kind. Eligible applicants are: fire departments; and national, regional, state, local, tribal and nonprofit interest organizations representing the interests of VOLUNTEER firefighters. Those interest organizations are eligible ONLY under the Recruitment and Retention (R&R) Activity - they are explicitly NOT eligible under the Hiring Activity. Conversely, career fire departments are NOT eligible under the R&R Activity. Subapplicants and subawards are NOT allowed at all. Maximum one application per activity. Scoring is two-stage: an automated pre-score based on responses to activity-specific questions in the online application (Application Narratives are NOT reviewed during pre-scoring) worth 50% of the total score under Hiring and 30% under R&R; then a Peer Review Panel of fire service representatives scoring the narrative, worth 50% under Hiring and 70% under R&R. Highest-ranking applications then go to a Technical Evaluation Process (technical review by a subject-matter expert plus FEMA Program Office review of costs, quantities, feasibility, eligibility, and recipient responsibility). FEMA reviews a random sample of applications to check for duplication including narrative statements and statistical data - all narrative statements must be specific and unique to the applicant, which is why nearly every criterion uses the word 'unique'. Boilerplate or grant-writer-templated narrative is an identified failure mode. The AOR must be a duly authorized current employee, personnel, official, staff, or leadership of the recipient with an email address unique to the recipient; consultants or contractors of the recipient are NOT permitted to be the AOR, and an application submitted by someone who is not current staff and duly authorized may be deemed ineligible. Federal funding may not supplant an existing activity or program, and FEMA will not fund projects, activities, or line items covered under a department's normal operating budget. Under R&R, applications requesting a Staffing Needs Assessment or Risk Assessment project are precluded from applying for additional R&R-related activities. Hiring Activity period of performance is 36 months, starting automatically after a default 180-day recruitment period regardless of whether the recipient has hired the requested firefighters. Subrecipients must submit short bios and resumes including entity type, organizational leadership, and board members with names and addresses; resumes are subject to approval.

PROTECT (23 U.S.C. 176) has two halves: a PROTECT Formula Program apportioned to State DOTs by formula with no application and no competition (see the FHWA PROTECT Formula Program Implementation Guidance), and this PROTECT Discretionary Grant Program, which IS a genuine open competition run through Grants.gov with a scored 25-page narrative. Eligible applicants for the Discretionary program under 23 U.S.C. 176(d)(2) are: (1) a State or political subdivision of a State (State includes DC and Puerto Rico); (2) an MPO; (3) a unit of local government; (4) a special purpose district or public authority with a transportation function, including a port authority; (5) an Indian Tribe as defined in 23 U.S.C. 207(m)(1); (6) a Federal land management agency that applies jointly with a State or group of States; (7) a multi-State or multijurisdictional group of entities described in (1) through (6). Private nonprofit organizations are NOT on that list and cannot apply directly - a nonprofit's only path is as a partner or subrecipient of an eligible public applicant. Per the FHWA PROTECT NOFO Q&A, public authorities with a transportation function can include public transportation and transit agencies. At-Risk Coastal Infrastructure Grants have a narrower rule (23 U.S.C. 176(d)(4)(C)(i)) requiring the applicant be in, or bordering on, the Atlantic, Pacific, or Arctic Ocean, the Gulf of Mexico, Long Island Sound, or one or more of the Great Lakes. BENEFIT-COST ANALYSIS: not required for Planning Grants; required for Resilience Improvement Grants UNLESS the project is in a qualifying Resilience Improvement Plan under 23 U.S.C. 176(e)(2); required for Community Resilience and Evacuation Route Grants. All relevant BCA files including spreadsheets must be submitted. Merit criteria are rated High / Medium / Low / Non-Responsive, then an Overall Merit Criteria Rating is assigned, then Priority Considerations are applied among projects of similar merit. Applicants are encouraged to include scalable project options. Must be registered in SAM.gov with a valid UEI before submitting; registration can take several weeks. FHWA will NOT request additional information to perfect incomplete applications. NOTE ON CFDA NUMBER: FHWA's own PROTECT NOFO cites Assistance Listing 20.205 (Highway Planning and Construction), not 20.284 - verify 20.284 against SAM.gov before relying on it. The FY 2024-2026 NOFO is a multi-year opportunity with separate closing dates per fiscal year: up to $876 million total, with up to $576 million for the FY 2024-2025 application period (closed February 24, 2025) and up to $300 million for a FY 2026 application period under the same NOFO.

special_requirements: NOT A STANDING PROGRAM - IT ONLY OPENS AFTER A DECLARED DISASTER AND A CONGRESSIONAL APPROPRIATION. There is no annual cycle. FTA publishes a Notice of Availability of Emergency Relief Funding (NAERF) in the Federal Register naming the specific disasters and calendar years covered, and applications are accepted only during that window. The FY 2023 NAERF (FTA-2023-009-TPM-ER, $212.3 million, 88 FR 18209, March 27, 2023) covered major declared disasters in calendar years 2017, 2020, 2021, and 2022 with a May 26, 2023 deadline; FTA reopened submissions for 90 days on August 2, 2023 for the remaining balance. NONPROFITS CANNOT APPLY DIRECTLY unless they are already an FTA direct recipient that provides or funds public transportation service. Verbatim eligibility: 'Public transportation agencies, States, territories, local governmental authorities, Indian tribes, and other FTA grant recipients that provide or fund public transportation service are eligible for Emergency Relief funding under the program.' Entities that generally receive transit funding directly from FTA may apply per the NAERF; public transit systems that are NOT FTA direct recipients (i.e., are subrecipients) but have incurred eligible expenses may receive Emergency Relief funding through a pass-through entity such as a State or designated recipient. So a nonprofit transit provider's access path is through its State DOT or designated recipient, not a direct application. Damage must stem from a FEMA major disaster declaration - applicants are pointed to fema.gov/disasters for declarations, Public Assistance designations, and incident periods. NO DOUBLE-DIPPING: transit systems that have been reimbursed by FEMA for emergency relief expenses, or that used FTA formula funds for them, may not apply for those same activities; ER funds may not reimburse costs covered by insurance proceeds or another Federal agency including FEMA. Cost share: maximum Federal share is 90 percent of net project cost, or 100 percent for a major declared disaster in an insular area (48 U.S.C. 1469a); applicants may request a waiver of the non-Federal share under 49 U.S.C. 5324(e)(3). Scalability: applicants are encouraged to identify scaled options with an appropriate minimum funding amount and a clear explanation of how the budget would be affected by a reduced award; FTA may award a lesser amount whether or not a scalable option is provided. Responses to the Local Financial Commitment, Project Implementation Strategy, and Technical/Legal/Financial Capacity criteria will NOT be used to disqualify applications - they inform technical assistance needs and match-waiver decisions - so Projects and Expenses is the criterion that actually gates the award. Supporting documents must be described AND referenced by file name in the appropriate response section of the supplemental form or they may not be reviewed. Do not enter 'N/A' or 'refer to attachment' in form fields. Emergency operating requests require the purpose of the service plus dates, hours, number and type of vehicles, and fare information; only net project costs may be reimbursed. Separately, FTA maintains an annual Emergency Relief Docket - a distinct mechanism through which grantees and subgrantees request temporary waiver of FTA administrative and statutory requirements after an emergency. That is regulatory relief, not funding, and should not be confused with this program.

special_requirements: 97.082 IS TWO SEPARATE NOFOs, AND THE NONPROFIT PATH IS THE SECOND ONE. FEMA's NEHRP State Assistance Grant Program runs (a) Individual State Earthquake Assistance (ISEA) and (b) Multi-State and National Earthquake Assistance (MSNEA), both under assistance listing 97.082, published as separate NOFOs on the same day each year. ISEA: 'This funding opportunity is available to states and territories classified as having a high or very high risk of earthquakes.' A NONPROFIT CANNOT APPLY FOR ISEA - only as a subapplicant/subrecipient of a state or territory. ISEA eligibility is not open-ended even among states: FEMA determines and publishes the classification annually in the State Assistance Target Allocation Plan, and the FY 2025 determination is based on Seismic Design Category per FEMA P-2082 / ASCE-SEI 7-22 as shown in the 2024 IBC SDC map plus at-risk population. A state is high risk if it has areas designated SDC-D or above with an at-risk population exceeding 50,000 (2020 Census), OR covers over 1,000 square miles of SDC-D or above. Such states get baseline funding plus a risk-based award computed from Annualized Earthquake Loss in FEMA P-366. Appendix C of the NOFO lists individual state cost share amounts, so ISEA behaves much more like a target allocation to qualifying states than an open competition - FY 2025 was $2,094,650 across 22 expected awards, range $50,000 to $963,000. ISEA requires a statutory non-federal cost share of 25 percent; participation is limited to states and territories that can provide it, though Insular Areas such as the U.S. Virgin Islands are exempt (48 U.S.C. 1469a(d) and OMB Controller Alert CA-23-04 require waiving match for Insular Area grants under $200,000). MSNEA IS THE ONE A NONPROFIT CAN APPLY TO DIRECTLY. Verbatim MSNEA eligibility: 'Nonprofit organizations as defined by Title 2 C.F.R Section 200.1' and 'Institutions of higher education as defined by Title 2 C.F.R. Section 200.1', restricted to those 'with a demonstrated capability and capacity to develop, promote and deliver national and/or multi-state seismic risk reduction activities referenced in Appendix C (Programmatic Information) and a demonstrated ability to work collaboratively with staff and leadership at the highest levels of state and federal governments.' MSNEA cost share is OPTIONAL, not required. FY 2025 MSNEA was $1,314,350 with awards of $100,000 to $300,000 and a period of performance of October 1, 2025 to March 31, 2027. MSNEA awardees are selected by a national review panel of FEMA NEHRP subject matter experts evaluating experience, proposed work plan, deliverable schedule, anticipated outcomes, and proposed budget. Both NOFOs use the identical program-specific document set (Work Plan Narrative, Master Schedule/Deliverable Table, Grant Budget, Logic Model, Statement of Work) and the same FEMA GO submission path, so the section list above applies to both. Other constraints: applicants may only propose activities listed in Appendix C - Programmatic Information; unallowable project types include real property and equipment procurement, international travel, construction and renovation costs, retrofits, and earth science related work. The budget must use Earned Value Management methodology reporting Budgeted Cost of Work Scheduled and Actual Cost of Work Performed, structured with Work Breakdown Structure cost categories, with activities correlating directly to the work plan master schedule and deliverable table. Funds will not be made available for obligation, expenditure, or drawdown until FEMA approves the applicant's budget and budget narrative. Subapplicants should not include foreign nationals or noncitizens; if they do, they must be properly vetted under 'staff American, stay in America' and security requirements. Applicants with system-related issues are supported only until 3:00 PM ET on the due date. FEMA published FY 2026 ISEA and MSNEA NOFOs on July 13, 2026 - re-check those for the current cycle.

special_requirements: THIS IS NOT A COMPETITION AT ALL - IT IS CONGRESSIONALLY DIRECTED SPENDING, AND THE WINNERS ARE NAMED IN THE NOFO BEFORE ANYONE APPLIES. Verbatim from the FY 2026 NOFO Section 7.B: 'FEMA regional staff will review all applications for compliance with program requirements. There is no selection process as all funding decisions are predetermined by Congress.' Section 7.F Merit Review Process: 'Not Applicable.' Section 7.G Final Selection: 'Not Applicable.' The projects are the earmarks (Congressionally Directed Spending) listed in the Joint Explanatory Statement accompanying the DHS Appropriations Act, and they are reprinted in Appendix 2 of the NOFO. Verbatim eligibility: 'Only State Administrative Agencies (SAAs), on behalf of state and local units of government, with identified projects in Appendix 2 of this NOFO are eligible to apply.' 'Subapplications and subawards are allowed only for the local units of government identified in Appendix 2 and will be coordinated/issued by the applicable SAA.' NONPROFITS CANNOT APPLY, AND NEITHER CAN A STATE OR LOCALITY THAT DOES NOT ALREADY HAVE AN EARMARKED PROJECT IN APPENDIX 2. Practically, the access path is not grantsmanship - it is getting a project into a congressional appropriations earmark in an earlier cycle. The IJ template adds: all prospective recipients of CDS funds, with the exception of tribal governments (tribes apply directly to FEMA), must apply through their State Administrative Agency, and each SAA sets its own internal submission deadline to allow time for state review. One application per state, territory, or tribe. Cost share: 25 percent non-federal of total project cost, cash or third-party in-kind, EXCEPT construction activities, which must be a cash (hard) match; the required cost share per project is fixed in the Appendix 2 project funding table; applicants must commit to the cost share for each activity at the time of application. The AOR must be a duly authorized current employee, personnel, official, staff, or leadership of the recipient with an email address unique to the recipient; consultants or contractors of the recipient are NOT permitted to be the AOR, and an application submitted by someone not current staff and duly authorized may be deemed ineligible. Subapplicants/subrecipients should not include foreign nationals or noncitizens; if they do, they must be properly vetted under 'staff American, stay in America' and security requirements. Subapplicants/subrecipients must submit short bios and resumes including entity type, organizational leadership, and board members with names and addresses; resumes are subject to approval. Recipients that are state, local, tribal, or territorial governments must ensure and maintain adoption and implementation of NIMS during the period of performance. An intergovernmental review may be required - contact the state's Single Point of Contact under Executive Order 12372. FY 2026 total was $82,957,854 across 27 expected awards, application due July 15, 2026.

special_requirements: Funding Opportunity Number USDA-AMS-TM-RFSI-C-23-0001. Assistance Listing 10.190. ELIGIBILITY: the only entities eligible for the USDA award are departments of agriculture in States and Territories - there is NO direct federal application path for businesses or nonprofits. Subaward-eligible entities: agricultural producers/processors or groups thereof; nonprofit organizations operating middle-of-the-supply-chain activities; for-profit entities operating middle-of-the-supply-chain activities that meet SBA small business size standards; local government entities; tribal governments; institutions such as schools, universities, hospitals bringing producers together for shared infrastructure. All applicant businesses and organizations must be domestically owned and facilities must be physically located in the 50 States, DC, Puerto Rico, USVI, Guam, American Samoa, CNMI, Palau, FSM, or the Marshall Islands. INELIGIBLE PRODUCTS (section 1.2.1): meat and poultry, wild-caught seafood, exclusively animal feed and forage products, fiber, landscaping products, tobacco, dietary supplements. INELIGIBLE ACTIVITIES (section 1.5.7): acquiring real property (including land purchases) or any interest therein; projects focused on meat and poultry processing or other ineligible agricultural products; activities that have received a Federal award from another Federal award program; expenses reimbursed under any Federal, State, or local government funding; projects already funded by another federal grant or subaward program may not receive funding for the same activities. MATCH: Infrastructure Grant recipients must contribute 50 percent of total proposed project cost; reduced to 25 percent for historically underserved farmers and ranchers or SBA small disadvantaged / women-owned / veteran-owned small businesses (self-certified in the application). No match for Simplified Equipment Only Projects. Program income and other Federal funds are an ineligible source of match. All matching contributions must be committed or secured at the time an applicant is recommended for an award. AWARD SIZE: Infrastructure Grants minimum $100,000, maximum $3,000,000; Simplified Equipment-Only Projects $10,000 to $100,000 (Fixed Price Grant, equipment purchases only, no facility upgrades or staffing). Indirect: NICRA honored if held, otherwise de minimis 10 percent of MTDC. Build America Buy America (BABA) applies.

special_requirements: FY2025 Funding Opportunity Number USDA-AMS-TM-FMPP-G-25-0005. SCORING: Alignment and Intent 25 points; Technical Merit 25; Achievability 25; Expertise and Partners 25; Fiscal Plan and Resources 25. Turnkey applications are scored on all criteria EXCEPT Alignment and Intent, with the remaining four carrying 25 points each. AMS may assign additional points for program priorities, geographic coverage/variety, and benefit to underserved communities. MANDATORY TEMPLATE: use of the AMS Project Narrative form is mandatory and 'Evaluation points will be deducted if the Project Narrative form is modified.' Do not use your own project narrative template; handwritten applications will not be accepted. Exceeding the page limit may disqualify the application. COST SHARE: 25 percent of the amount of Federal funds requested, cash and/or in-kind from non-Federal sources. Cannot be Federal funds of any kind or program income. Cannot double-count toward another Federal grant's cost share. All cost sharing must be committed or secured at the time an applicant is selected - an award will not be issued unless all cost sharing over the life of the grant is secured; anticipated funds not in place by project start cannot count. Signed Letters of Verification required for EACH cash and/or in-kind resource. ELIGIBILITY: applicants must be domestic entities owned, operated, and located within the 50 states, DC, Puerto Rico, USVI, Guam, American Samoa, CNMI, or Tribal Governments. Eligible entity types: Agricultural Business or Cooperative; Community Supported Agriculture (CSA) Network or Association; Economic Development Corporation; Food Council; Local Government; Nonprofit Corporation; Producer Network or Association; Public Benefit Corporation; Regional Farmers Market Authority; Tribal Government. Only the applicant must meet eligibility - partners and collaborators do not, and may be private or public, for-profit or nonprofit. INELIGIBLE ACTIVITIES (section 3.3.5) - projects are not eligible if the proposed activities: are not focused on direct producer-to-consumer marketing; are for agricultural production related expenses including crop production and purchase of farm equipment, tools, materials, supplies; include training, labor or other activities related to agricultural production including harvesting, crop rotation, and planting techniques; benefit only one agricultural producer, vendor, or individual; are to buy land, or for construction of a building or structure; intend to register, train, and/or educate customers on Food Assistance Programs (such as SNAP, WIC) other than providing information about how they can use those benefits at the market; depend upon the completion of another project or the receipt of another grant; include legal fees and other costs associated with establishing a business or organization; duplicate activities already funded by another Federal award program, including the Local Food Promotion Program. UNALLOWABLE COSTS include building and construction, contributions/donations, fundraising activities, production related cost, and purchasing/leasing/upgrading systems or equipment used to process SNAP, WIC, or other Federal nutrition benefit programs. Special purpose equipment capped at $6,500 for food safety equipment. Fringe above 35 percent requires justification. REGISTRATION: UEI, TIN, and active SAM.gov registration required; AMS warns SAM registration can take up to 4 weeks and Grants.gov AOR registration up to 4 weeks. Projects that are duplicates of a previous grant will not be selected for funding.

special_requirements: MOST IMPORTANT ELIGIBILITY CONSTRAINT - MANDATORY STATUTORY PARTNERSHIP: per CAA sec. 138(b)(3), eligible applicants are ONLY (1) a partnership between two community-based nonprofit organizations (CBOs), or (2) a partnership between a CBO and one of: a federally recognized Tribe, a local government, or an institution of higher education. A single organization CANNOT apply alone. A CBO must be either the Lead Applicant or the Statutory Partner in EVERY Statutory Partnership - there cannot be a statutory partnership of, for example, a local government and an institution of higher education. If selected, the Lead Applicant must enter a subaward with the Statutory Partner. OTHER ELIGIBILITY EXCLUSIONS: nonprofit organizations described in Section 501(c)(4) that engage in lobbying activities as defined in Section 3 of the Lobbying Disclosure Act of 1995 are NOT eligible to apply. Foreign nonprofit organizations cannot qualify as a CBO. For-profit Alaskan Native Corporations are not eligible under the CBO definition. States, territorial governments, and international organizations cannot legally be Statutory Partners (they may only be Collaborating Entities). The CBO must have a geographic presence or connection in, or relationship with, the specified community the projects are intended to benefit - national or statewide CBOs must demonstrate that connection. INELIGIBLE ACTIVITIES: projects for community or Tribal relocation activities are not eligible and will not be reviewed; EPA will not consider any application that includes projects exclusively designed to conduct scientific research; EPA will not consider any application requesting funding for assessment, removal, or remediation of Superfund sites. Including ineligible projects may render the ENTIRE application ineligible, not just that portion. FUNDING CAPS: Track I cannot request more than $20 million; Track II cannot request more than $3 million; applications exceeding these will be rejected. All grants must be completed within three years of award per CAA sec. 138(b)(1). A Track I application for a Target Investment Area (TIA) can only address ONE TIA. Track I applications for pollution monitoring or awareness must also include an associated remediation, implementation, or infrastructure pollution reduction project. Applications must be submitted in English only - applications in other languages will not be reviewed. Lead Applicants may submit no more than two eligible applications and receive no more than two awards. MATCH: 'No cost-sharing or matching is required as a condition of eligibility under this NOFO.' Applications submitted outside of Grants.gov, or after the deadline, will be deemed ineligible. SAM.gov registration required.

MOST IMPORTANT ELIGIBILITY CONSTRAINT: per 7 CFR 4280.112(a) the applicant must be an AGRICULTURAL PRODUCER or RURAL SMALL BUSINESS at the time of application. NONPROFIT ORGANIZATIONS AND UNITS OF GOVERNMENT ARE NOT ELIGIBLE APPLICANTS - 4280.112(c) explicitly names 'a non-profit entity' as an example of an ineligible applicant, and bars a newly formed special-purpose entity with substantially the same ownership as a sole ineligible end-user. FUNDING: grant will not exceed 25 percent of eligible project costs (so a 75 percent applicant contribution is structurally required and cannot be waived); certain IRA-funded categories allow up to 50 percent. COST TIMING TRAP: costs incurred before the Agency's acknowledgement of a complete and eligible application and completion of environmental review are considered INELIGIBLE PROJECT COSTS - starting construction early can disqualify costs or the project. SUBMISSION: one original application to the USDA RD State Office Energy Coordinator for the state where the project will be located, or via grants.gov. Active SAM.gov registration and UEI required before submitting; Financial Assistance General Certifications and Representations must be completed in SAM. special_requirements: Governed by 7 CFR part 1778, authorized by Section 306A of the Consolidated Farm and Rural Development Act. ELIGIBILITY (7 CFR 1778.6): grants may be made to public bodies AND private nonprofit corporations serving rural areas - this program DOES have a direct nonprofit pathway, unlike most water infrastructure programs. Public bodies include counties, cities, townships, incorporated towns and villages, boroughs, authorities, districts, other political subdivisions of a State, Indian tribes on Federal and State reservations, and other federally recognized Indian Tribal groups in rural areas. HARD DISQUALIFIER: 'Any entities responsible for willfully or purposely fouling a drinking water supply are not eligible to be the recipients of an award under this program.' TIMING ELIGIBILITY GATE: the decline must have occurred within TWO YEARS of the application filing date (or, for imminent decline, be likely to occur within ONE YEAR) - this is an eligibility condition, not a scoring factor. RESTRICTIONS ON USE OF FUNDS (7 CFR 1778.10): may not assist any city or town with a population in excess of 10,000 inhabitants; may not assist a rural area with median household income in excess of the statewide nonmetropolitan median household income (5-year ACS data); may not finance facilities that are not modest in size, design, and cost or not directly related to correcting the potable water quantity or quality problem; may not pay loan or grant finder's fees; may not pay annual recurring operational expenses; may not pay rental for equipment or machinery owned by the rural community; may not purchase existing systems; may not refinance existing indebtedness (except short-term debt under 1778.9(h)); may not make reimbursement for projects developed with other grant funds; may not finance facilities that are not for public use. MAXIMUM GRANTS (7 CFR 1778.11): up to $1,000,000 for a significant decline in quantity or quality; capped at $150,000 for repairs, partial replacement, or significant maintenance on an established system. NO MATCH REQUIRED: 'Grants under this part... shall be made for 100 percent of eligible project costs.' SET-ASIDE: at least 70 percent of grants must go to 1778.11(a) projects; at least 50 percent of appropriated funds must go to rural areas with populations not in excess of 3,000. Costs incurred within six months before the application was filed may be eligible (1778.9(h)). Subject to Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

base_forms: No standard competitive grant application package. narrative_sections: Formal request to the State Conservationist for assistance (must be submitted within 60 days of the natural disaster occurrence, or 60 days from the date when access to the sites becomes available);A statement that the sponsors understand their responsibilities and are willing to pay its cost-shared percentage;Information pertaining to the natural disaster, including the nature, location, and scope of the problems and the assistance needed;NOTE: after the sponsor's request, NRCS (not the sponsor) prepares the Damage Survey Report (DSR) and the economic/environmental documentation required by 7 CFR 624.6(d). special_requirements: Governed by 7 CFR part 624. MOST IMPORTANT ELIGIBILITY CONSTRAINT - MANDATORY GOVERNMENTAL SPONSOR: the sponsor 'must be a State or political subdivision thereof, qualified Indian tribe or tribal organization, or unit of local government.' Explicitly: 'Private entities or individuals may receive assistance only through the sponsorship of a governmental entity.' A nonprofit, a private forestland owner, or a landowner CANNOT apply directly - they must find a governmental sponsor. SPONSOR OBLIGATIONS: contribute their share of project costs (cash, in-kind services such as labor, equipment, design, surveys, contract administration and construction inspection, or a combination); obtain any necessary real property rights, water rights, and regulatory permits; agree to provide for any required operation and maintenance of the completed emergency measures. COST SHARE: Federal contribution may not exceed 75 percent of construction cost of emergency measures; up to 90 percent if NRCS determines the area qualifies as a limited resource area. The sponsor share is structural and is not described as waivable. INELIGIBLE ACTIVITIES AND LANDS (7 CFR 624.6(b)(2)): EWP assistance will NOT be used to perform operation or maintenance; will NOT be used to repair, rebuild, or maintain private or public transportation facilities, public utilities, or similar facilities; will NOT be provided on any FEDERAL LANDS if such assistance is found to augment the appropriations of other Federal agencies; is NOT available for repair or rehabilitation of nonstructural management practices such as conservation tillage. If the same type of natural event occurs within a 10-year period and a structural measure has been installed or repaired twice in that period using EWP assistance, assistance is limited to sites eligible for floodplain easement purchase. Recovery measures eligible under the FSA Emergency Conservation Program are excluded. EWP assistance is only available when landowners, land managers, or land users document they have exhausted or have insufficient funding or other resources. If the sponsor wants an increased level of protection beyond the EWP practice, the sponsor pays 100 percent of the upgrade cost. TIMING: NRCS will not fund activities undertaken by a sponsor prior to the signing of the agreement between NRCS and the sponsor. FUNDING PRIORITIES (ranked): exigency situations; sites with a serious but not immediate threat to human life; sites where buildings, utilities, or other important infrastructure are threatened - with additional weight for federally listed threatened and endangered species or critical habitat, National Register cultural sites, prime farmland supporting high value crops, wetlands, major water quality effects, and unique habitat.

special_requirements: Governed by 7 CFR part 622 (Public Law 83-566 Watershed Protection and Flood Prevention Operations). MOST IMPORTANT ELIGIBILITY CONSTRAINT - MANDATORY STATE ROUTING WITH A GOVERNOR-LEVEL VETO: per 7 CFR 622.21, 'The governor or designated State agency will approve or disapprove the application. If disapproved, no further action is required of NRCS.' The application never reaches NRCS on its merits if the state disapproves it. Applications go to the State Single Point of Contact under Executive Order 12372 first. SPONSOR ELIGIBILITY (7 CFR 622.10): all watershed plans must be sponsored by entities legally organized under State law, or by any Indian Tribe or Tribal organization, having the authority to carry out, operate, and maintain works of improvement. Sponsors of plans incorporating nonstructural or structural measures must, individually or collectively, have (i) THE POWER OF EMINENT DOMAIN and (ii) the authority to levy taxes or use other adequate funding sources to finance their share of project cost and all operation and maintenance costs. The eminent domain requirement does not apply to Indian Tribes or Tribal organizations. This effectively excludes nonprofits, private landowners, and most non-governmental entities - only a taxing/condemning local governmental body or a Tribe can sponsor. PROJECT ELIGIBILITY LIMITS (7 CFR 622.11): the watershed must not exceed 250,000 acres; no single structure may provide more than 12,500 acre-feet of floodwater detention capacity nor more than 25,000 acre-feet of total capacity; the project must produce substantial benefits to the general public, communities, and groups of landowners; and it CANNOT be installed by individual or collective landowners under alternative cost-sharing assistance. Structural water resource projects must have the greatest net national economic benefits consistent with protecting the environment unless the Secretary grants an exception. Sponsors must commit to use their powers and authority to carry out and maintain the project as planned.

special_requirements: Funding Opportunity Number EPA-R-OAR-CPRGT-23-09, Assistance Listing 66.046. Alaskan Native Corporations (ANCs) are not eligible for direct grants under this program based on the CAA section 302(r) definition of 'Indian tribe.' FUNDING RANGE: applications requesting less than $2 million or in excess of $500 million are not eligible and will not be reviewed. INELIGIBLE EXPENSES: applications that include ineligible expenses are ineligible to receive funding for such costs, and inclusion of ineligible expenses may render the FULL application unsuitable for funding. Applications must support EPA Strategic Plan Goal 1 'Tackle the Climate Crisis,' Objective 1.1. A group applying as a coalition must designate a lead applicant, and coalition members must provide letters of intent. An eligible applicant may submit only one application as the lead applicant. Active SAM.gov registration required and the submitter must be associated with the applicant organization's SAM.gov account.

special_requirements: FOA numbers DE-FOA-0002740 (round 1) and DE-FOA-0003195 (round 2). Assistance Listing 81.254. TWO-STAGE GATE: a Concept Paper is a REQUIRED first step - an eligible Concept Paper must have been submitted for each Full Application, and only compliant Concept Papers may proceed. A Concept Paper is compliant only if it complies with the content and form requirements in Section IV.C of the FOA and is successfully uploaded in Exchange by the deadline. MOST IMPORTANT CONSTRAINT - COST SHARE VARIES SHARPLY BY TOPIC AREA AND IS STATUTORY: Topic Area 1 (Grid Resilience Grants, BIL 40101(c)) requires the recipient to MATCH 100 PERCENT of the Federal grant amount - i.e. a 1:1 match - except SMALL UTILITIES, which must match only 1/3 of the Federal grant. A small utility is defined as an entity that sells no more than 4,000,000 MWh of electricity per year, and 30 percent of Topic Area 1 funding is set aside for small utilities. Topic Area 2 (Smart Grid Grants, BIL 40107) requires cost share of at least 50 percent of total project costs. Cost share must come from NON-FEDERAL sources unless otherwise allowed by law. ELIGIBILITY DIFFERS BY TOPIC AREA - this is the trap: Topic Area 1 eligible entities are limited to electric grid operators, electric storage operators, electricity generators, transmission owners or operators, distribution providers, and fuel suppliers. NONPROFITS AND UNIVERSITIES ARE NOT ELIGIBLE UNDER TOPIC AREA 1. Topic Area 2 eligibility is much broader and DOES include for-profit entities, non-profit and not-for-profit entities, state and local governmental entities, Tribal nations, and institutions of higher education. INELIGIBLE UNDER TOPIC AREA 1: a new electric generating facility; a new large-scale battery-storage facility that is not used for enhancing system adaptive capacity during disruptive events; and CYBERSECURITY. Topic Area 2 award maximum is capped at $50 million, with exceptions of $100 million for projects aggregating multiple utility service territories and $250 million for projects deploying advanced conductors for transmission line capacity improvement at scale. An entity may submit more than one Concept Paper and Full Application provided each describes a unique, scientifically distinct project. DOE strongly encourages submission at least 48 hours before the deadline.

Eligibility is limited to states (and authorized state agencies) that have or are seeking EPA authorization to operate a hazardous waste program in lieu of the federal program. There is NO nonprofit, local government, university, or private-sector application pathway - consistent with our data showing 129 of 141 awards to state government. Grants and cooperative agreements are RENEWED ANNUALLY provided all requirements are met; there is no open competition to enter. Separately, a state changing its authorized program scope must submit program revision application materials under 40 CFR part 271, which EPA does publish materials for.

special_requirements: ELIGIBILITY IS TRIBAL-ONLY - closed to nonprofits, universities, states, and local governments as prime applicants. Eligible: federally recognized Tribes on the current Federal Register list under the Federally Recognized Indian Tribe List Act of 1994, plus authorized Tribal organizations as defined at 25 U.S.C. 5304(l). Other entities may participate only as sub-awardees. Tribal organization proposals are reviewed and ranked SEPARATELY from Tribal proposals. For the First Time Awardees Set Aside, only federally recognized Tribes (NOT Tribal organizations) are eligible, and 'Consultants are not eligible as sub-awardees, as the intent of this funding is to build internal Tribal staff capacity.' TRIBAL RESOLUTION REQUIRED: all proposals must have Tribal resolution(s) to enter an ISDEAA Self-Determination contract under Title I, or a cover letter for a Self-Governance compact under Title VI. A Tribal organization proposing to serve multiple Tribes must have a resolution from every Tribe it services; proposals to host trainings or fund travel for other Tribes must append Tribal Resolutions from all benefitting/participating Tribes. AWARD CAPS (FY23): Category 1 Planning max $250,000; Category 2 Implementation max $4,000,000; First Time Applicants max $250,000; Habitat Restoration and Adaptation no maximum; RMP Coordinator max $150,000 per year for up to three years. No award minimum. LIMIT of two planning awards and one implementation and/or construction award per funding Category per Tribe. SCORING: each activity standard set is worth up to 100 points, with Supplemental Points adding up to 15 more, explicitly 'intended to create equity across awards'. Broad Benefits supplemental points REQUIRE letters of support or resolutions from the Tribes that will be involved or benefit. NO MATCH REQUIRED - budget totals 'should not include Tribal match, in-kind, or leveraged funds from other agencies and/or organizations.' Because awards are made under P.L. 93-638, TCR awards CAN be used as the federal match for other federal programs. INCOMPLETENESS CURE: an incomplete proposal received at least two weeks before the deadline may be returned with an explanation, and the Tribe may fix and resubmit before the deadline. DISALLOWED COSTS include stipends, international travel, legal or contracted negotiation fees, entertainment and artwork, contingency funds greater than 10 percent, 'Miscellaneous' or 'other' funds, and establishing or operating a Tribal office or general office equipment; laptop/computer setup capped at $5,000 each; speaker fees and honorariums capped at 10 percent of total costs; food at remote training locations capped at the lesser of $17,500 or 7 percent of the requested amount. Contract Support Costs (CSC) are added AFTER award and must NOT be included in the proposal. Requests above a Category maximum will not be considered for review. FUNDING CONTINUITY CAVEAT: the RFP states BIL funding is slated through FY2026 and IRA funding through FY2024, and 'There is no assurance that TCR will be funded in subsequent years.' FOIA: material submitted may be disclosable under FOIA.

special_requirements: TWO FINDINGS HERE CHANGE ELIGIBILITY, NOT JUST WORDING. (1) THIS IS NOT A COMPETITIVE GRANT PROGRAM. The guide states plainly: 'Compatible Use and Installation Resilience grants are not competitive.' You cannot simply apply. Access is gated behind a nomination and approval sequence: a Military Department nominates an installation (annual call, typically in the Spring) OR a state or local government submits a community self-nomination to the Program Activity Lead; OLDCC assigns a Project Manager; the PM drafts a Project Directive establishing conformity with program authorities under 10 U.S.C. Section 2391; the Director approves it; a site visit follows (sometimes virtual); the PM and Program Activity Lead then recommend proceeding via an internal Determination and Findings requiring Director approval coordinated with the Office of Secretary of Defense General Counsel; and only then, quote, 'you, as the applicant, and with support from the installation, are invited to officially apply for the grant.' A self-nomination may include: Point of Contact; Description of actual/potential compatibility or resilience issue; A description of the proposed project; A description of the anticipated role of the installation(s) in the plan and concurrence with the proposal. (2) NONPROFITS ARE NOT ELIGIBLE. The eligible entities are exactly: states, counties, municipalities, other political subdivisions of a state, special purpose units of a state or local government, other instrumentalities of a state or local government, and tribal nations. If the organization is not readily identifiable as a state or local government it must attach a concise written legal opinion on letterhead from an attorney licensed in that state opining that the applicant is an instrumentality of state or local government and what inherently governmental functions it performs. THRESHOLD DETERMINATION: entities are eligible only if the OLDCC Director determines either (a) encroachment of the civilian community is likely to impair the continued operational utility of the military installation, OR (b) threats to the military installation are likely to impair its continued operational utility. COST SHARE: 'typically 10 percent non-Federal share which could be contributed in a variety of ways.' INSTALLATION CONCURRENCE IS EFFECTIVELY MANDATORY - the installation must recommend and support the nomination, and for an Installation Resilience nomination the installation must provide a summary of existing and planned resiliency efforts with source documentation (Installation Energy and Water Plans, evaluations using the Department of Defense Climate Assessment Tool, Comprehensive Plans with resilience incorporated, or hazard risk modelling); if the installation has not begun resiliency planning activities, OLDCC 'may defer the nomination until they are underway.' The community must act as fiscal agent, staff the effort with appropriate expertise, and organize participants 'to speak with one voice.' Typical project duration 12 to 18 months; proposed start date ideally within 3 months of application; start dates begin the first day of a month and end dates the last day of a month. Typical study area 1 to 5 miles around the installation boundary, not necessarily contiguous. Geospatial data is a REQUIRED deliverable. Competitive procurement is required for contractual costs per 2 CFR 200.

narrative_sections: SCORING CRITERIA (100 points + 10 preference points), from the EPIC Application Manual. The Project Narrative (Attachment 2) must respond to each criterion and sub-criterion in order.;1. Technical Merit (15 points) -- The proposed project provides a clear and concise description of the technological, scientific knowledge advancement, and/or innovation that will overcome barriers to achieving the State's statutory energy goals, Describes the competitive advantages of the proposed technology over state-of-the-art (e.g., efficiency, emissions, durability, cost), Provides the proposed technical specifications and describe how the project will meet or exceed the technical specifications by the end of the project, Describes the technology readiness level (TRL) the proposed technology has achieved and the expected TRL by the end of the project, Describe how the proposed model/tool/study will be used by key parties (e.g., policymakers, project developers, other researchers), Describes the advantage of the proposed model/tool/study over that currently being used by key parties, Provides information described in Section I.C.;2. Technical Approach (25 points) -- The application describes the technique, approach, and methods to be used in performing the work described in the Scope of Work, The Scope of Work identifies goals, objectives, and deliverables, details the work to be performed, and aligns with the information presented in Project Narrative, The application identifies the reliability that the project and site recommendations as described will be carried out if funds are awarded, Identifies and discusses factors critical for success, in addition to risks, barriers, and limitations (e.g., loss of demonstration site, key subrecipient). Provides a plan to address them, Discusses the degree to which the proposed work is technically feasible and achievable within the proposed Project Schedule, Describes the technology transfer plan to assess and advance the commercial viability of the technology, Provides a clear and plausible M&V plan that describes how energy savings and other benefits specified in the application will be determined and measured, Provides information documenting progress towards achieving compliance with the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), Provides information described in Section I.C.;3. Impacts and Benefits for California IOU Ratepayers (20 points) -- Explains how the proposed project will benefit California IOU ratepayers and provides clear, plausible, and justifiable (quantitative preferred) potential benefits. Estimates the energy benefits including: annual electricity savings (kilowatt-hour), energy cost reductions, peak load reduction and/or shifting, infrastructure resiliency, and/or infrastructure reliability. In addition, estimates the non-energy benefits including: GHG emission reductions, air pollutant emission reductions (e.g., NOx), water savings and associated cost reductions, and/or increased safety, States the timeframe, assumptions with sources, and calculations for the estimated benefits, and explains their reasonableness. Includes baseline or 'business as usual' over timeframe, Explains the path-to-market strategy including near-term (i.e., initial target markets), mid-term, and long-term markets for the technology, size and penetration or deployment rates, and underlying assumptions, Identifies how model outputs and/or strategic outcomes will benefit key parties.;4. Team Qualifications, Capabilities, and Resources (15 points) -- Evaluations of ongoing or previous projects including project performance by applicant and team members will be used in scoring for this criterion, Identifies credentials of applicant and any subrecipient and sub-subrecipient key personnel, including the project manager, principal investigator and technology and knowledge transfer lead, Demonstrates that the project team has appropriate qualifications, experience, financial stability and capability to complete the project, Explains the team structure and how various tasks will be managed and coordinated, Describes the facilities, infrastructure, and resources available that directly support the project, Describes the team's history of successfully completing projects in the past 10 years including subsequent deployments and commercialization.;Subtotal: Total Possible Points for criteria 1-4 = 75. Minimum Passing Score for criteria 1-4 is 70% or 52.50.;5. Budget and Cost-Effectiveness (10 points) -- Budget forms are complete for the applicant and all subrecipients, Justifies the reasonableness of the requested funds relative to the project goals, objectives, and tasks, Justifies the reasonableness of direct costs (e.g., labor, fringe benefits, equipment, materials & misc., travel, subrecipients), Justifies the reasonableness of indirect costs (e.g., overhead, facility charges (e.g., rent, utilities), burdens, subrecipient profit, other like costs), Justifies how the proposed project, including the amount of match funds, optimizes the use of CEC funds to achieve program objectives, Justifies the appropriateness of match funds with respect to the project's potential risks and benefits, including level of commitment, type of match (e.g., cash, in-kind), sources, and match funding replacement strategy.;6. CEC Funds Spent in California (10 points) -- Projects that maximize the spending of CEC funds in California will receive points as indicated in the table. Calculated, not written.;7. Ratio of Direct Labor to Indirect Costs (5 points) -- Calculated by formula: Total Direct Labor / (Total Direct Labor + Total Fringe + Total Indirect + Total Profit), multiplied by the maximum possible points.;Total Possible Points for Criteria 1-7 = 100. Minimum Passing Score for Criteria 1-7 is 70% or 70.00 points.;PREFERENCE POINTS: Disadvantaged & Low-Income Communities (10 points) -- Applications proposing projects located in and benefiting low-income and/or disadvantaged communities within IOU service territories may qualify for additional preference points. Identifies how the proposed project will lead to increased deployment of the technology or solution to benefit disadvantaged and/or low-income communities, including specific entities that will receive these benefits, Identifies how the proposed project will have a positive economic impact on low-income and/or disadvantaged communities including customer bill savings, job creation, partnering and contracting with micro- and small-businesses, and economic development, Describes potential negative impacts or risks of the proposed technology or solution to disadvantaged and/or low-income communities and how they will be assessed and mitigated, Describes how the proposed project will increase access to clean energy or sustainability technologies within disadvantaged and/or low-income communities, Identifies and describes how community input will be solicited and considered in the design of the project, and how outreach and engagement will be conducted during project implementation, Includes letters of support from technology partners, community-based organizations, environmental justice organizations, or other partners.

narrative_sections: PROGRAM STATUS WARNING -- READ FIRST. The APGP is NOT currently soliciting. Round 2 was cancelled. Verbatim from the agency: 'Due to California's budget constraints, funding for Round 2 of the Adaptation Planning Grant Program (APGP) has unfortunately been canceled.' The sections below are the published Round 1 requirements (application window January 6 to March 31, 2023) and are the only APGP application structure the agency has ever published. They are a reliable guide to what a future round would likely look like, but they are not an open opportunity.;PROJECT NARRATIVE -- the five graded narrative questions, verbatim from the Round 1 Guidelines summary of Full Application components (word counts as published):;Project Vision & Priorities (250 words);Community Need & Adaptive Capacity (750 words);Co-Benefits (250 words);Community Partnership (500 words);Budget Justification (250 words);FULL PROMPT TEXT FOR EACH NARRATIVE QUESTION, verbatim from Appendix E: Application.;Project Vision & Priorities -- 'Present the Vision Statement. Include the project approach, priority goals, objectives, and aspirations of your proposed project. (250 words)';Community Need & Adaptive Capacity -- 'Provide any or all of the following, using any of the sources listed in Section A "Consideration of Vulnerable Communities" of the APGP Grant Guidelines (750 words): 1. An overview of any existing information about the proposed project area's vulnerable communities, including population characteristics, locations, and other known factors contributing to vulnerability. 2. How the vulnerable communities have been involved in the proposed project to date (or, if this has not yet been feasible, the plan for how they will be involved from application submission date onward). 3. How the project will address the unique needs, and enhance the adaptive capacity of, vulnerable communities.' Plus: 'Describe known climate change-related issues and possible solutions in the project region, as well as gaps in this knowledge the project will address, including any or all of the following: 1. Any existing information available on current and future climate change impacts, and gaps in known information. 2. Information on historic conditions, such as hazards faced by the community in the past. 3. How the proposed planning project will expand on existing knowledge and fill information gaps on climate change vulnerability, impacts, and/or adaptation solutions and build community resilience to climate change.';Co-Benefits -- 'Describe how the proposed project will prioritize strategies and outcomes that provide climate change adaptation co-benefits (such as social equity, greenhouse gas mitigation, economic, and/or environmental co-benefits). (250 words)';Community Partnership -- 'Describe the partnership structure, including roles, responsibilities, and why this specific group of organizations is well suited to carry out the proposed planning activities of the proposed project. Include details on previous history working together if applicable, if this is an emerging partnership, share what aspects of this new partnership will set the group up for success. (500 words)';Workplan and Budget -- 'Provide a high-level budget justification that summarizes the overall project costs. Explain how the requested budget is aligned with the proposed Work Plan and reflects the overall project objectives and program goals. Applicants may choose to organize the budget items under the eligible cost categories for the APGP. (250 words)';ADDITIONAL DOCUMENTATION, verbatim: Application Workbook (Applicant Summary; Work Plan; Budget), Letters of Support (up to three), Documentation that the application meets all eligibility requirements described in the Eligible Applicants.;PHASE 1 (pre-application) -- 'Request for Application Materials: APGP Intent Survey', short-answer items including G. Lead Applicant Contact Information and H. Co-Applicant(s) Contact Information. Completing the Intent Survey was the only way to receive the individualized SharePoint folder containing the actual application materials.

Maps, figures, and pictures may be included as part of the responses. Bullets, lettering, and underline may be used; avoid excessive formatting. This definition does not include state agencies.' special_requirements: GEOGRAPHIC RESTRICTION (critical): applicants must be based in or supporting efforts in Minnesota, North Dakota, South Dakota, or the 23 Native nations that share that geography. Applicants outside this region are ineligible. Eligible entity types: 501(c)(3) nonprofits; government entities including schools; coalitions or collaboratives (only one organization may receive the grant); organizations working with a fiscal sponsor that has 501(c)(3) status. Rolling - applications welcome at any time throughout the year, online application open year-round. NOT a formal LOI process, but the Foundation explicitly asks anyone interested to CONTACT THEM FIRST before applying, so they can hear the idea and answer questions and the applicant does not spend time on an application that is not a fit.
